extraction.name: MMMU: Massive Multi-discipline Multimodal Understanding and Reasoning
extraction.description: A benchmark of 11,550 college-level multimodal questions designed to evaluate expert-level perception, subject knowledge, and reasoning in multimodal foundation models. It covers six disciplines, 30 subjects, 183 subfields, and 30 heterogeneous image types, with interleaved text and images, multiple-choice questions, and concise open-ended questions.
extraction.creator: Xiang Yue; Yuansheng Ni; Kai Zhang; Tianyu Zheng; Ruoqi Liu; Ge Zhang; Samuel Stevens; Dongfu Jiang; Weiming Ren; Yuxuan Sun; Cong Wei; Botao Yu; Ruibin Yuan; Renliang Sun; Ming Yin; Boyuan Zheng; Zhenzhu Yang; Yibo Liu; Wenhao Huang; Huan Sun; Yu Su; Wenhu Chen
extraction.citeAs: Xiang Yue et al. MMMU: A Massive Multi-discipline Multimodal Understanding and Reasoning Benchmark for Expert AGI. arXiv:2311.16502v4, 13 June 2024.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Subjects were selected from common university majors where visual inputs commonly provide valuable information, yielding 30 subjects across six disciplines. Over 50 university students specializing in these subjects, including coauthors, manually collected multimodal questions from textbooks and online resources and created new questions using their expertise where necessary. They were instructed to diversify sources, respect copyright and licensing restrictions, avoid sources prohibiting copying or redistribution, and prefer questions whose answers were not immediately available. Approximately 13,000 questions were initially collected before quality control.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Explanations were annotated only when available. The final dataset contains explanations for 2,035 questions, representing 17.62% of the questions.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: College exams, quizzes, textbooks, lecture materials, free online resources, and other study materials. Some questions were newly created by annotators based on their subject expertise.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Authors corrected formatting deviations and typographical errors. Each sample was stored in a separate JSON file using the naming convention subject_{Number}.json; images used image_{QuesNum}_{ImageNum}.png. Image file paths were inserted into question, option, or explanation text to represent interleaved text and images.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Lexical overlap and source URL similarity were used to identify suspected duplicate questions, which authors reviewed and removed when confirmed. Coauthors checked standardized formatting and typos. Authors classified questions as very easy, easy, medium, or hard; approximately 10% classified as very easy were excluded because they did not meet the benchmark's intended difficulty. The final dataset was divided into 150 development questions, 900 validation questions, and 10,500 test questions.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: University students with relevant subject expertise annotated question type, question text, multiple-choice options, correct answer, image types, difficulty, and explanations when available. Guidelines required English, college-level questions containing images, with unambiguous answers expressible as a single option or short response. Authors assigned difficulty categories during quality control. A secondary review team vetted annotations for quality and adherence to guidelines, and the protocol called for regular audits of random samples.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: A custom web interface for data annotation and verification developed by Tianyu Zheng.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Ambiguous or unclear instances were to be flagged for detailed review and collaboratively examined in team meetings to establish a standardized annotation approach. Secondary reviewers checked annotation quality and consistency. Analysis of 150 randomly sampled GPT-4V errors attributed 2% to annotation errors.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Over 50 university students, including coauthors, specializing in the benchmark's various disciplines and subjects.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: Xiang Yue led the dataset release. The annotation protocol calls for regular audits of random dataset samples to maintain quality and consistency. A live-updating model leaderboard is available on the benchmark website. The paper provides a version change log documenting updated model results and corrections; it does not specify a dataset update schedule or deprecation policy.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The annotation protocol instructs annotators to avoid collecting questions containing any private information and to comply with privacy laws and ethical standards in data handling.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The benchmark is intended to help monitor progress toward Expert AGI. The paper discusses the possibility that Expert AGI could reach the substitution threshold for human labor in many industries, creating significant risks of job displacement and economic disruption, and therefore emphasizes the intellectual and societal importance of monitoring this progress.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The paper explicitly acknowledges that the manual curation process may carry biases.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The focus on college-level subjects is not sufficient for testing Expert AGI. There is no direct mapping between MMMU performance and the 90th percentile of skilled adults, and college exams are not the only tasks an AGI should address. Subjects such as law and linguistics were excluded because sufficient relevant multimodal problems were difficult to find. Annotation inaccuracies were identified in the error analysis.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Evaluation and benchmarking of multimodal foundation models' perception, subject knowledge, and reasoning across college-level disciplines. The development set provides five questions per subject for few-shot or in-context learning demonstrations; the validation set supports hyperparameter selection and prompt engineering; the test set supports final evaluation. The paper reports zero-shot and few-shot evaluations using micro-averaged accuracy. MMMU is intended to guide model development and monitor progress toward Expert AGI, but should not be treated as a sufficient standalone test of Expert AGI.
